expansion:
A. 8 to 10 years is the keyed answer. In anisometropic amblyopia, unequal refractive input during early visual development causes the brain to favour the clearer dominant-eye image; patching the dominant eye compels use of the amblyopic eye while cortical visual development remains responsive. The clinically important sensitive period extends approximately to 8 to 10 years, so a 6-year-old can still benefit substantially from aggressive occlusion treatment (not taken from the course material). The lecture identifies occlusion as “Treatment of amblyopia” and shows opaque and translucent spectacle occluders (L29, slide 32), but it does not give the age range. Indeed, it explicitly states: “NO REGIMEN IS GIVEN” and “no age limit” (L29, slide 32).

B. 2 to 4 years is wrong because this is within the highly responsive early period, not its approximate upper limit. Treatment should be instituted promptly at this age if amblyopia is detected, but benefit is not restricted to this narrow age range (not taken from the course material).

C. 12 to 14 years is wrong as the usual approximate age at which visual-cortical plasticity provides significant benefit from conventional amblyopia treatment is earlier, around 8 to 10 years. Some older children may still show improvement, but this does not make 12 to 14 years the expected cut-off for substantial benefit (not taken from the course material).

D. 18 years is wrong because routine occlusion therapy is much less predictably effective once the childhood sensitive period has passed; adult cortical plasticity does not support 18 years as the approximate age limit tested here (not taken from the course material).

The associated refractive lecture calls anisometropia “the most common cause of amblyopia in children” (L7,8, slide 83), but likewise supplies no occlusion regimen, critical period, or age limit.
objective: Identify that amblyopia patching has significant benefit while visual cortical plasticity persists, approximately until 8 to 10 years of age.
